pages.title: Hunt
pages.summary: Generate detections for a threat group, one or more CVEs, or a list of ATT&CK techniques. Fill in one field and press Generate.

sections.title: Four ways to start
sections.what: Hunt starts from a threat, Analyse from a report, Profile from a company, and Research from a question such as "who targets finance in Europe?".
sections.when: Choosing the tab is choosing your starting point. Pick the one that matches what you've been handed.

sections.title: Threat group
sections.what: Type a group's ATT&CK name or any alias (APT29, Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard). Shikari collects every technique the group uses, directly, through its campaigns and through its software, and builds a detection for each.
sections.when: A group is named in a briefing, an incident or a sector advisory and you need coverage for its whole playbook, not one indicator.

sections.title: CVEs and ATT&CK techniques
sections.what: Enter CVE IDs to build exploit-request, runtime-shell, behaviour and IOC-sweep queries from the NVD, advisories and public exploits. Or enter technique IDs to hunt them across every group that uses them. Browse the last 30 days lists new CVEs with KEV status.
sections.who: Vulnerability and SOC teams for CVEs; detection engineers for techniques.
sections.when: A CVE is being exploited before you can patch, or a red-team report or gap analysis gives you a list of techniques.

sections.title: Options
sections.what: Merge sub-techniques into their parent, test queries against containerised SIEMs (Auto-validate), add LOLBAS, LOLDrivers and LOLRMM indicators, merge public detection rules (OSINT Enhancement), and score against them (OSINT Comparison).
sections.when: The defaults suit most hunts. Turn on OSINT Comparison when a group's techniques have few indicators in ATT&CK.

sections.title: Start from a hypothesis
sections.what: Describe what you think an adversary is doing in your own words; Shikari maps it to ATT&CK and generates the detections and correlations for it.
sections.when: You have a hunch from an alert, an incident or the news, but not yet a group or technique ID.

pages.title: Analyse a report
pages.summary: Build detections from a threat report, by URL or as a file. You review every technique and indicator before anything is generated.

sections.title: A report's URL
sections.what: Paste a blog post or advisory. Shikari extracts the ATT&CK techniques, the commands, and the indicators of compromise, defanged ones included, then shows them for review.
sections.who: Threat intelligence analysts and detection engineers.
sections.when: A vendor publishes an intrusion write-up relevant to you. Feed cards open here with the URL filled in.

sections.title: Upload a file
sections.what: PDF, text, Markdown, JSON, CSV, XLSX, DOCX or YARA. Drag it onto the box or choose it.
sections.when: The report is a paid or shared PDF, or the site blocks automated fetches.

sections.title: Options
sections.what: The same enrichment options as Hunt. The IOC sweep leaves out known-good infrastructure such as public DNS resolvers and the platforms' own domains.
sections.when: Turn off OSINT Enhancement when you want detections built only from what the report says.

pages.title: Profile a company
pages.summary: Start from a company instead of a threat. Shikari works out its sector, geography and exposure, recommends the groups most likely to target it, and hunts the ones you choose.

sections.title: The company's domain
sections.what: Enter a primary domain. Shikari reads public sources (Wikidata, DNS, certificate transparency, Shodan InternetDB, HIBP breach metadata) to build the profile and an exposure map. Nothing is harvested.
sections.who: Threat intelligence analysts and security managers.
sections.when: Onboarding a new client or business unit, or answering "who is likely to come after us?".

sections.title: OSINT sources and keys
sections.what: Every source the profile uses, with a toggle. Most need no key; Shodan, SecurityTrails, HIBP and GitHub keys add coverage.
sections.when: Profiles look thin. A key adds sources; a toggle switches one off without deleting the key.

pages.title: Research groups
pages.summary: Find threat groups by keyword, then see which ATT&CK techniques they share, so a detection that covers several of them comes first.

sections.title: Keywords
sections.what: Words matched against each group's ATT&CK description, a country, sector or technology. AND or OR combines them; Attributed or Targeted reads a country as the group's origin or its victim.
sections.when: The question is "who targets finance in Europe?" rather than "detect APT29".

sections.title: Add groups by name
sections.what: Add particular groups to the keyword matches. Up to 20 are used.
sections.when: Your intelligence names groups the keywords don't find.

sections.title: Consolidate or hunt
sections.what: Consolidate Techniques builds a table of which groups use each technique. Hunt Threat Groups and Hunt Techniques fill the Hunt tab, so a technique several groups share is hunted once.
sections.when: You have a shortlist of groups and limited time. Shaded rows (used by more than one group) are the best value.

pages.title: Results
pages.summary: Where every hunt, report and profile ends. Its detections, correlations, attack flow, the anatomy of the attack and a threat briefing, all built without AI.

sections.title: Threat briefing
sections.what: How many of the group's techniques you detect, the weakest stage of its attack, and the gaps to close first, ranked by how early they come and how many correlations they're in.
sections.when: Reporting coverage against a named threat, or deciding what to build next.

sections.title: Detections
sections.what: One card per detection, grouped by SIEM, with its technique, tactics, severity, confidence and query. Badges show OSINT enrichment, reference queries and changed mappings, and each card's quality grade (A–F), false-positive risk and, when it's not low, run cost. Hover a badge for the reasons.
sections.when: Reviewing what to deploy. Copy a query straight into your SIEM to test it.

sections.title: Correlations
sections.what: Detections chained into one query that fires when several steps of an attack happen on the same host or account within a time window. Three-technique chains are high-confidence leads.
sections.when: Single-technique alerts are too noisy. A correlation fires far less often and means more when it does.

sections.title: Cross-vendor playbooks
sections.what: Chains that span two or more of your SIEMs, laid out stage by stage with each SIEM's query and the fields to join them on.
sections.when: Your endpoint and network telemetry live in different SIEMs.

sections.title: Attack flow
sections.what: The group's techniques by tactic, each marked with the SIEMs that detect it or No detection, with correlations drawn as links. Rearrange it and download it as STIX Attack Flow.
sections.when: Briefing a team on how an attack unfolds and where you're blind.

pages.title: Library
pages.summary: Every detection and correlation you've saved, your working set. Search, filter, tag and export it.

sections.title: Metrics
sections.what: Totals across the Library, detections, correlations, techniques and tactics, with an estimate of analyst time saved.
sections.when: Reporting on the detection programme.

sections.title: Filters
sections.what: Search names, techniques and query text, and narrow by group, SIEM, tactic or technique.
sections.when: Finding the detection that should have fired for an alert, or everything you have for one technique.

sections.title: Detections and bulk actions
sections.what: The saved cards. Tick several to tag, export (JSON, CSV, XML, Word, PDF) or delete them together.
sections.when: Handing a set of detections to another team, or tidying after a review.

sections.title: ATT&CK flows and anatomy
sections.what: Links to the attack flow and anatomy of each saved group, report or CVE.
sections.when: Going back to a group you covered weeks ago.

pages.title: Detections as code
pages.summary: Commit a run's detections to git, diff two runs, and plan a push into a SIEM's own rule store.

sections.title: Export a run to git
sections.what: Writes each detection to a stable path per group and SIEM, and commits. Detections that need a data source you don't ingest are listed as excluded.
sections.when: You review and deploy rules through pull requests.

sections.title: History and diff
sections.what: Pick two commits and see added, removed and changed detections.
sections.when: After a Regenerate on a new ATT&CK release, to see exactly which queries moved.

sections.title: Push to a SIEM
sections.what: Builds the Defender XDR or Google SecOps rule payloads a push would send, as a dry run.
sections.when: Checking what a deployment would create before wiring it up.

pages.title: Coverage
pages.summary: Which ATT&CK techniques you have queries for, by tactic, technique and platform, and where one SIEM covers what another doesn't.

sections.title: Totals
sections.what: Queries, techniques covered, and queries per SIEM.
sections.when: A one-line answer to "how much of ATT&CK do we cover?".

sections.title: Filters
sections.what: Narrow by number of queries, SIEM, tactic, platform or a search.
sections.when: Looking at one platform (macOS, cloud) or one SIEM's coverage.

sections.title: Coverage by tactic and the matrix
sections.what: One card per tactic, and the full ATT&CK matrix coloured by how many queries each technique has. The layers switch between your reference queries and the detections you've saved.
sections.when: Planning the next quarter's detection work, or showing coverage on a familiar picture.

sections.title: Cloud coverage
sections.what: ATT&CK's cloud techniques by provider (AWS, Azure, GCP, identity and SaaS) and which SIEMs have a detection over that provider's logs. Gaps only lists what's missing.
sections.when: Moving workloads into a cloud, or checking control-plane logging is earning its keep.

sections.title: By technique, platform and gaps
sections.what: Compact cards per technique or platform, exportable as CSV, and Coverage Gaps, techniques covered in one SIEM but not another.
sections.when: Mid-migration between SIEMs, or when two teams run different ones.

pages.title: Flows
pages.summary: The attack flow of every group, report and CVE in your Library, what you can and can't detect across each attack.

sections.title: Choose a flow
sections.what: Pick a saved group, report or CVE; Open results goes to its Results page.
sections.who: Threat hunters, purple teams and security managers.
sections.when: Walking through an attack with people who don't read queries.

sections.title: The flow
sections.what: Each column is a tactic, each card a technique with the SIEMs that detect it or No detection. Arrows are correlations. Drag cards between tactics, or draw your own links.
sections.when: Answering "if they got this far, would we see the next step?".

sections.title: Controls
sections.what: Filter by SIEM, hide undetected techniques, draw the correlations, focus on selected cards, turn the layout round, undo, and download as STIX Attack Flow.
sections.when: Cutting a large flow down to the part you're discussing.

pages.title: Anatomy
pages.summary: How an attack runs in plain words, in the style of the DFIR Report's workflow diagrams, ways in, toolkit, actions and where it goes, each step marked detected or not.

sections.title: Choose a group or CVE
sections.what: Every threat group and CVE in your Library. This page counts every detection you have for it, from any run.
sections.who: Threat intelligence analysts and security managers.
sections.when: Explaining a threat to an executive audience without ATT&CK IDs.

sections.title: The workflow
sections.what: Ways in (exploits, phishing, credentials), its toolkit, what it does once in, and the cloud, messaging and storage services it uses. Teal steps are mostly detected, red mostly not. Select a step for the detail behind it.
sections.when: Briefing on a group's tradecraft rather than its technique list.

pages.title: Threat Feed
pages.summary: The last seven days of technical threat research from vendor and government sources, tagged with the industries, nations and products involved. No AI.

sections.title: Filters
sections.what: Your industries, your technology stack, opportunistic or financial activity, both, or everything. Posts naming only products you don't run are left out by default.
sections.who: Threat intelligence analysts and SOC leads.
sections.when: The Monday-morning read of what's new and relevant.

sections.title: Watchlists
sections.what: Saved searches (a group, a CVE, a vendor). Shikari collects every six hours and flags new matches on the Intel menu, and can email them.
sections.when: Tracking a campaign or actor over weeks without checking by hand.

sections.title: The wall
sections.what: One card per post with source, summary and tags. Analyse in Shikari turns a post into detections.
sections.who: Threat intelligence analysts and detection engineers.
sections.when: A post matches your stack or industry. Analysing it takes a minute.

sections.title: Sources
sections.what: Each source and its last collection. Administrators can add RSS or Atom feeds.
sections.when: A source you rely on isn't there, or one has stopped.

pages.title: Cyber Powers
pages.summary: National cyber capability on a world map, by IISS tier, by how firmly ATT&CK attributes groups to each country, and by who is targeted.

sections.title: The map
sections.what: Three views (Nations, Groups, Targets). Hover a country for its tier, attribution, motivations and groups. Your country is green.
sections.who: Threat intelligence analysts and security managers.
sections.when: Geopolitical briefings, and putting a nation-state advisory in context.

sections.title: Countries by tier
sections.what: The countries in each tier, confidence level or target ranking, with their flags.
sections.when: A quick reference for a board paper.

pages.title: STIX/TAXII & MISP
pages.summary: Take STIX bundles, TAXII collections and MISP events as a hunt input, and export a finished run as STIX or a MISP event.

sections.title: Import intelligence
sections.what: Upload or paste a STIX 2.1 bundle or MISP event, poll a TAXII collection, or query a MISP instance. Credentials are used for that request only.
sections.when: Intelligence arrives from an ISAC, a sharing community or a TIP rather than a blog post.

sections.title: Export a run
sections.what: A STIX 2.1 bundle with techniques, indicators and the detections themselves, or a MISP event with galaxies and attributes.
sections.when: Sharing what you built back to your community or into a TIP.

pages.title: Catalogue and company review
pages.summary: Every company profiled so far, and each one's review, the profile, its exposure map and the groups recommended for it.

sections.title: Profile summary
sections.what: Company, industry, location, hosting and a risk score, from public sources.
sections.when: Checking the profile is right before generating. A CDN or parent company can mislead it.

sections.title: Exposure map
sections.what: What an attacker can see before they act, IPs, networks, mail and its spoofability, subdomains, exposed services, known CVEs and breach metadata, linked back to the domain.
sections.who: Security managers, attack-surface and red teams.
sections.when: Attack-surface reviews, and before a penetration test.

sections.title: Generate detections
sections.what: The recommended groups in columns, each with its likelihood of targeting this organisation. Tick the ones to hunt.
sections.when: Turning a profile into coverage for the threats that matter to that company.

pages.title: MITRESaw
pages.summary: The ATT&CK procedure data behind Shikari's briefings and detections, every group's techniques, how each reaches the group, and the indicators in the procedure text.

sections.title: The procedures
sections.what: The ATT&CK version and build. Update collects only the groups the latest release changed; Full rebuild collects all of them.
sections.when: After an ATT&CK release.

sections.title: OSINT repositories
sections.what: The public detection-rule repositories and LOL datasets Shikari searches while generating, with each one's status.
sections.when: OSINT enrichment looks thin. Check every repository is ready.

sections.title: Procedures table
sections.what: Search and filter every procedure by group, technique, tactic and attribution (the group's own, a campaign's or its software's). Download CSV or XLSX.
sections.when: Checking why a group is linked to a technique, with the evidence.

pages.title: Emulate
pages.summary: Which logs record each ATT&CK technique, from attacks recorded in public labs, with your detections' indicators checked against those recordings. Nothing is sent to your SIEM.

sections.title: Plan an emulation
sections.what: Pick a group, CVE or technique and Shikari assembles a plan, the best recorded dataset per technique, the matching Atomic Red Team test and the log sources to collect. Export it as a run sheet or MACAT TOML.
sections.when: Before an emulation exercise, to agree what will run and what should be seen.

sections.title: Recordings and the indicator check
sections.what: How many recordings are available and whether detections can be checked against them.
sections.when: Checking the telemetry data is ready on this machine.

sections.title: Your lab
sections.what: Create and manage Docker, Tart and UTM machines from inside Shikari, start, stop, snapshot, revert and set them up.
sections.when: Recording your own telemetry rather than relying on public labs.

sections.title: Recorded telemetry
sections.what: Every recording by technique, group or data source, with the event types it captured.
sections.when: Deciding which log source a detection should be built on.

pages.title: Assessments
pages.summary: Test cases built from the groups that matter to you, and campaigns that record what each test did and what the defence saw, VECTR-style.

sections.title: New assessment
sections.what: A campaign with a target, an operator and a run date, holding test cases from the Threat library.
sections.when: Planning an exercise.

sections.title: Campaigns
sections.what: Record red (executed, failed, blocked) and blue (not logged, logged, alerted, prevented) per technique. Logged but no alert offers a hunt for that technique. Export CSV or an ATT&CK Navigator layer.
sections.when: During and after an exercise, to show what changed.

pages.title: Manual
pages.summary: Write detections from techniques and procedures you supply, one technique at a time.

sections.title: Group description
sections.what: An optional line about the group or your hypothesis, kept with the run.
sections.when: Recording why the run exists for whoever audits it later.

sections.title: Technique entries
sections.what: Choose a technique and its tactics, and list what was observed, one procedure per line. Commands, paths, registry keys and tool names become indicators. Append each, then Submit.
sections.when: A group ATT&CK doesn't know, or your own intelligence from an incident.

pages.title: Regex
pages.summary: Test a regular expression against your own text and check it for the SIEM it will run in. Everything runs in your browser.

sections.title: Expression and flavour
sections.what: The pattern, its flags, and the SIEM or language it's for. Defender XDR and SecOps run in RE2, Splunk in PCRE2, and Elastic matches the whole value.
sections.when: Any regex headed for a production rule.

sections.title: Test string
sections.what: Paste command lines, paths or log lines. Matches and capture groups are highlighted as you type.
sections.when: Checking against real samples, including near-misses that shouldn't match.

sections.title: Checks
sections.what: Errors and warnings for the chosen flavour, single backslashes in Windows paths, unescaped dots, empty matches, catastrophic backtracking.
sections.when: Before the SIEM finds the problem for you.

sections.title: Use it in a query
sections.what: The pattern written into a query for each SIEM, escaped for its strings.
sections.when: Moving a pattern between SIEMs.

pages.title: Agents
pages.summary: A model working in a loop with Shikari's tools, repairing queries, triaging reports, sweeping coverage gaps, auditing and tuning the Library. Every step is shown and kept.

sections.title: The agents
sections.what: Detection repair, Ask Shikari with tools, Intel triage, Coverage sweep, Library audit and Detection tuning. Each says what it needs and what it does.
sections.when: Repetitive review work that follows clear rules.

sections.title: Run one
sections.what: Choose the agent, its input and the model. Actions that change something wait for your approval unless you untick it.
sections.when: After a big run, let the repair agent fix only what the checks flag.

pages.title: Environment
pages.summary: What your organisation runs, applied to every hunt and to the Threat Feed.

sections.title: SIEMs, industries and technology stack
sections.what: The SIEMs to generate for, the industries the Feed keeps, and the products in your estate. Hunts leave out what can't happen there.
sections.when: First thing after installing. Every hunt is quicker and closer to your estate afterwards.

pages.title: API keys
pages.summary: AI providers, OSINT sources and SIEM credentials, stored encrypted. All optional.

sections.title: Keys and assignments
sections.what: A cloud provider's key or a local model's URL, which model answers Ask Shikari and which generates, a cap on AI calls per run, and keys for OSINT sources and SIEMs.
sections.when: Turning on AI-assisted generation, or adding OSINT coverage for company profiles.

pages.title: System configuration
pages.summary: Settings that apply to every user, for administrators.

sections.title: Correlation parameters
sections.what: The relevance score a correlation needs, how many each SIEM gets, and how often one technique can start a chain.
sections.when: Results carry too many correlations to review, or too few.

sections.title: Webhooks
sections.what: URLs Shikari posts to when a hunt finishes or fails, or a watchlist finds new posts, signed with a secret shown once. Send test checks the receiver.
sections.when: A ticket, chat message or pipeline should follow a hunt without anyone watching it.

pages.title: Help
pages.summary: What Shikari does with each kind of input, what it's for, and the frequently asked questions. The guide and these tips are in the Help menu too.

sections.title: What it does
sections.what: The inputs Shikari takes and what it makes of them.
sections.when: Explaining Shikari to a colleague.

sections.title: Use it for
sections.what: The jobs Shikari is built for, from hunting a named group to profiling an organisation.
sections.when: Deciding where to start.
